n: Eliphaz continues: Go ahead and call out — will any heavenly being take your side? He suggests no one in heaven will support Job’s complaint.
Resentment destroys the fool. Eliphaz hints that Job’s angry lament is the kind of thing that ruins a person.
Eliphaz has seen fools seem to prosper and put down roots, but he pronounced their home cursed, and it soon fell.
The fool’s children find no safety and are crushed in court with no one to defend them. These words would wound Job, whose children had just died.

f.g: Defeated in court — legal cases were heard at the city gate.

n: The hungry eat the fool’s harvest, even taking it from among thorns, and thieves swallow his wealth — another painful echo of Job’s recent losses.
Trouble doesn’t just sprout from the ground like weeds — it has a cause.

f.w: cometh not forth of the dust
f.g: Doesn’t arise by itself, without a reason.

n: Human beings are born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward from a fire. This famous line has been quoted for centuries as a description of mortal life.

f.g: Literally “sons of Resheph” — sparks or flames flying up.

n: Eliphaz’s advice: If I were you, I would turn to God and bring my case to Him. Good counsel — though Job will indeed do so, more boldly than Eliphaz expects.
God does great and unsearchable things, wonders beyond counting.
He sends rain to water the earth and the fields — a life-giving gift in a dry land.

f.w: Who giveth rain upon the earth

n: He lifts up the lowly and brings those who mourn to safety. God reverses fortunes — a theme also seen in Hannah’s and Mary’s songs.

f.w: To set up on high those that be low

n: God frustrates the schemes of clever plotters so they cannot succeed.

f.w: disappointeth the devices of the crafty

n: He catches the wise in their own cleverness. Paul quotes this line in the New Testament — the only time Job is quoted there.

f.w: He taketh the wise in their own craftiness

n: The schemers stumble around in broad daylight as if it were night — confused and lost.
God rescues the poor from the sword of cruel words and from the hands of the powerful.

f.g: From the “sword” of their slanderous mouths.

n: So the poor have hope, and injustice is silenced.
Eliphaz now offers a true principle: blessed is the one God corrects, so don’t reject His discipline. But he assumes Job’s suffering must be correction for sin.

f.w: happy is the man whom God correcteth

f.g: Hebrew Shaddai, a name for God used often in Job.

n: God wounds, but He also binds up; He strikes, and His hands heal. A beautiful truth about God’s healing power.

f.w: he woundeth, and his hands make whole

n: “Six troubles, yea, seven” is a Hebrew number pattern meaning “every trouble.” God will protect you in all of them.

f.w: in six troubles: yea, in seven
f.g: A Hebrew way of saying “in every possible trouble.”

n: In famine and in war, God will save you from death.
He will protect you from slander and from fear of disaster.

f.g: The whip of slander and gossip.

n: You will even laugh at destruction and famine and not fear wild animals. Eliphaz paints a picture of perfect security.
You will be at peace with the stones of the field — they won’t ruin your crops — and wild animals will live peacefully with you. It is an image of creation in harmony.

f.w: in league with the stones of the field
f.g: Your fields will be free of stones that ruin farming.

f.w: the beasts of the field shall be at peace with thee

n: Your home will be safe, and when you check your flocks, nothing will be missing.

f.g: Here likely meaning “shall miss nothing” — find nothing lacking.

n: Your children will be many, like the grass of the earth. To a man who had just buried ten children, this promise must have stung.

f.w: thine offspring as the grass of the earth

n: You will reach the grave in ripe old age, like a sheaf of grain gathered at harvest time. Ironically, this does come true for Job in the end (Job 42:16-17).

f.g: A bundle of harvested grain stalks.

f.w: Thou shalt come to thy grave in a full age

n: Eliphaz concludes confidently: we have studied this, and it is true — accept it for your own good. His sincere but rigid theology leaves no room for innocent suffering.
